newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors trim charges against spymaster.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors trim charges against spymaster.

text.p: German prosecutors said on Tuesday they were dropping charges of treason and extortion against Markus Wolf as the trial of the legendary East German spymaster neared its conclusion.
But a spokeswoman for a state court in Duesseldorf said Wolf was still facing charges of abduction for three cases from the 1950s and 1960s.
She said prosecutors had dropped the treason and extortion charges in order to speed up the trial. They will make their closing arguments next Wednesday.
The suave 73-year old Wolf ran East Berlin's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years. He has rebutted the charges.
The trial is a last bid by prosecutors to bring to book the elusive figure dubbed "the man without a face" as his western counterparts for decades had little idea what he looked like.

Wolf was convicted of treason in the same Duesseldorf courtroom in 1993. But Germany's highest court overturned the decision in 1995, saying Wolf could not be convicted of spying on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.

This time prosecutors charged Wolf with crimes under East German law. The charges relate to intelligence work in the 1950s and 1960s. Wolf said he was not directly involved in the 1962 kidnapping of a former officer from the Ministry for State Security (Stasi) who had fled to Austria.
Prosecutors say the officer, Walter Thraene, and his girlfriend were abducted, beaten unconscious and spirited back to East Germany, where they served lengthy prison terms.

Wolf ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside Chancellor Willy Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
